He pointed out that the engineering industry has a 'rainy season' mechanism for typhoons and heavy rain that allows construction periods to be postponed, and that extreme heat should also be taken into account. He urged the government to take the lead in following up. He also suggested that the government should adjust its work heat stress warning standards to suit outdoor workers, and advocated for prosecution of employers who violate the rules.

Hot weather has once again drawn attention to the working conditions of outdoor workers, with 'occupational safety men' bearing the brunt. Ho Ping-tak, who has been in the industry for many years, has expressed various views on the scaffolding trade. The government has in recent years sought to introduce metal scaffolding. In extremely hot weather, the most obvious difference between metal and bamboo scaffolding is temperature — but just how great is the difference?

Metal scaffolding at construction sites: 'can easily reach 60-something, even 70 degrees'

Ho Ping-tak said that, generally speaking, metal scaffolding at construction sites is built using iron tube frames. Compared with the suspended aluminium frames used for small-scale repair works, the materials are heavier and more heat-conductive. An iron tube awaiting installation left in direct sunlight, with no nearby shade, 'could easily reach 60-something, even 70 degrees.'

Personally witnessed seven workers, five suffering heatstroke

Ho Ping-tak once visited a metal scaffolding construction site and, standing on the rooftop holding a thermometer, took a reading — 54.6 degrees. He has also visited a site at Anderson Road, where seven people were working on the floor and five showed symptoms of heatstroke. He went on to point out that metal scaffolding absorbs far more heat than traditional bamboo scaffolding, and that the hardship endured during extremely hot weather is correspondingly greater.

Sites offering ice cream and fruit to beat the heat — Ho Ping-tak: only large-scale sites do so. Ho Ping-tak noted that although some construction sites now install thermometers or wind speed displays around the area, and some companies even treat workers to ice cream, fruit, and herbal tea to cool down, giving the impression that working conditions are slowly improving, these benefits are limited to large-scale sites. Companies that take the initiative to require workers to rest after the Labour Department issues a 'work heat stress warning' are even rarer. In reality, workers still have to 'figure things out on their own' — bringing their own neck fans, fan jackets, or freezing large water bottles into blocks of ice to bring to work.

He mentioned that when the Labour Department established the 'work heat stress warning' in 2023, frontline workers were thrilled, thinking 'finally the Labour Department is willing to speak up and fight for this heat warning on behalf of us frontline workers.' He said workers had originally expected the warning to function like typhoon or rainstorm warnings, bringing construction sites to a temporary halt. 'Who would have thought it has been issued over 200 times, yet not once has it reached the red level or ordered people to stop work.' What is worse, even during the recent 'highest temperature on record,' only a yellow warning was in effect.

Ho Ping-tak pointed out that temperatures in Central, at construction sites, and on hillsides all vary. Though he is not a professional, he questioned whether the mechanism for issuing work heat stress warnings should be adjusted to suit the conditions of outdoor workers. 'At some construction sites it gets to over 50 degrees, so when so-called experts formulate these measures, shouldn't they experience it for themselves? It's not about sitting in an air-conditioned room and assessing data. I believe that to prove whether any theory works, practice is what matters most.'

Rainy season allows construction delays — Ho Ping-tak urges government to take the lead in treating heat stress the same way

Ho Ping-tak further pointed out that many companies in the industry have a 'rainy season' concept, meaning that after work is halted due to typhoons or heavy rain, companies are allowed to postpone delivery deadlines. He explained that this practice exists because in the past Hong Kong might have had five or six typhoons a year, and in severe weather 'bamboo can slip, and couplers can come loose in one's grip.' However, with extreme heat, workers also become dizzy, yet there is currently no similar consideration. When facing tight construction schedules, 'when it's too hot and you want a break, but the construction period doesn't change, the concrete pouring schedule doesn't change, a lot of brothers and workers are actually quite helpless.'

He believes the current heat stress warning has fallen into a situation of 'following it is a matter of人情 (favours), not following it is a matter of道理 (principle).' Because construction delays are penalised on a daily basis, employers who do the maths find that 'even earning everything still isn't enough to pay the fines (from the developer)' and naturally choose to exploit workers, leaving workers in a passive position. He suggested the government consider making rest periods under the warning mandatory, with penalties for main contractors who fail to comply. The government should also take the lead by allowing construction periods to be extended at discretion without penalties when work is halted due to extreme heat, so that contractors will follow suit.

Labour Party Legislative Council member Lam Chun-sing also agreed, saying that even if the threshold for issuing heat stress warnings were revised, 'I don't think it would be red every day? Perhaps only 8 to 10 of the hottest days,' and he believed the impact on overall construction would be limited.
